**Stop competing on the checklist; change the evaluation criteria.** Checklists reward breadth, incumbents always win breadth.

**Moves, in order of leverage:**

1. **Get in before the RFP is written.** Whoever shapes criteria wins. If you're arriving at a finished checklist, the incumbent (or their champion) wrote it, so qualify out or reframe.

2. **Replace checklist w/ a job-based bake-off.** Propose: "pick your 3 real workflows, time both tools end-to-end." Measure time-to-first-value, steps, lines of config, p95 latency, whatever you win on. Devs trust a hands-on trial over a matrix.

3. **Reframe their breadth as cost.** 200 features = config surface, upgrade pain, training, seat price for stuff unused. Ask: "which of these checked boxes will you use in 12 months?" Typically <20%.

4. **Pick 1 wedge, win it 10x.** Narrow segment or use case where the incumbent is structurally bad (legacy architecture, pricing model, enterprise-first UX). The weakness must be one they can't fix w/o hurting their core business; otherwise they patch it in 2 quarters.

5. **Position as complement where possible.** "Keep X for A, use us for B" removes the rip-and-replace objection & the head-to-head matrix. Expand later.

6. **Plant landmine criteria.** Give champions questions the incumbent answers badly: "setup time w/o professional services?", "cost at 10x usage?", "can 1 engineer own it?"

7. **Concede openly.** "We don't do X, Y, Z, on purpose." Builds credibility, signals focus, pre-empts the incumbent's FUD.

**Qualify harder:** if the buyer is procurement-led, wants checklist coverage & has no dev champion, walk. Your win rate there is approx. 0 & it burns sales cycles.

**Diagnostic for you:** review the last 10 losses. If lost on features nobody uses, it's a positioning problem (above fixes it). If lost on 1-2 features repeatedly, it's a table-stakes gap, build them.

Share the category & incumbent, I'll get specific on wedge & landmine questions.
